CLOUDPOINT GEOSPATIAL
Field Safety Guide
Policies, Procedures & Best Practices for Field Personnel
About This Guide
This guide establishes safety requirements and best practices for Cloudpoint Geospatial employees
performing field mapping, data collection, surveying support, asset inventory, inspections, and related
outdoor work activities. All Cloudpoint field personnel are required to review, understand, and follow the
policies contained herein.
All employees have the authority and responsibility to stop work whenever conditions become
unsafe. No employee will be disciplined for exercising stop-work authority in good faith.
KEY CONTACTS
Emergency: 911
Cloudpoint Main Office: (877) 377-8124
Supervisor: ________________________ Phone: ________________________
Cloudpoint Geospatial | Internal Use Only | Page 1

Cloudpoint Geospatial | Field Safety Guide cloudpointgeo.com | (877) 377-8124
1. General Field Safety Expectations
Before beginning any field assignment, all Cloudpoint personnel must complete the following pre-field
checklist:
PRE-FIELD CHECKLIST
• Review project scope and site-specific hazards
• Verify weather conditions and forecasts for the work area
• Ensure mobile phone or communication device is fully charged
• Carry all required PPE for the assignment
• Inform supervisor of work location and expected return time
• Confirm vehicle is fueled and in safe operating condition
• Review emergency procedures and identify nearest medical facilities
Employees shall never take unnecessary risks to complete a project. If conditions become
unsafe at any point, stop work and notify your supervisor immediately.
2. Required Personal Protective Equipment (PPE)

The following minimum PPE is required for all Cloudpoint field assignments. Additional PPE may be
required based on project-specific hazards or client site requirements.
PPE Item Requirement / Notes
High-Visibility Vest ANSI Class 2 or higher when working near traffic
Safety Glasses Required at all times in field environments
Closed-Toe Footwear Sturdy; appropriate for terrain conditions
Weather-Appropriate
Clothing
Layers for cold; breathable fabrics for heat
Gloves When handling equipment or in rough terrain
Hard Hat When required by site conditions or client requirements
3. Traffic and Roadway Safety
Cloudpoint Geospatial | Internal Use Only | Page 2

Cloudpoint Geospatial | Field Safety Guide cloudpointgeo.com | (877) 377-8124
Working near roads presents one of the highest risks to field personnel. All requirements below are
mandatory with no exceptions.
Requirements
• Wear high-visibility apparel at all times when working near traffic
• Remain alert to moving vehicles at all times
• Face traffic whenever practical
• Use sidewalks and pedestrian pathways when available
• Maintain a safe buffer from active traffic lanes
• Avoid standing in blind spots, curves, intersections, or high-speed areas
• Use traffic control devices only when trained and authorized
• Never enter active traffic lanes unless specifically authorized and protected by traffic control
measures
Parking
• Park in a safe location away from traffic whenever possible
• Activate hazard lights when parked near roadways

• Exit vehicles on the side away from traffic whenever feasible
IF CONDITIONS BECOME UNSAFE
• Stop work immediately
• Relocate to a safe area
• Contact your supervisor before resuming
4. Terrain and Ground Conditions
Field personnel frequently encounter uneven and unpredictable terrain. Common hazards include slips,
trips, falls, hidden holes, loose rock, steep slopes, mud, ice, and snow.
Safe Practices
• Watch footing continuously — never assume ground is stable
• Avoid running in field environments
• Test unstable ground before proceeding
• Use extra caution on slopes and embankments
• Maintain three points of contact when climbing
• Avoid working on terrain beyond your physical capability
• Use designated trails and access routes whenever possible
Cloudpoint Geospatial | Internal Use Only | Page 3

Cloudpoint Geospatial | Field Safety Guide cloudpointgeo.com | (877) 377-8124
Employees should stop work if terrain conditions present an unreasonable risk and notify their
supervisor before proceeding.
5. Weather Safety
Heat
• Stay hydrated throughout the workday
• Take breaks in shaded or cool areas regularly
• Monitor for heat stress symptoms: dizziness, headache, excessive sweating, nausea, confusion
• Notify your supervisor immediately if symptoms develop
Cold
• Dress in appropriate layers for conditions
• Protect hands, feet, and exposed skin
• Monitor for signs of hypothermia and frostbite
• Seek warmth and contact your supervisor if symptoms develop
Lightning
If thunder is heard or lightning is observed:
• Stop field activities immediately
• Seek shelter in a hard-topped vehicle or substantial building
• Do not stand near isolated trees, poles, fences, or metal structures

• Wait at least 30 minutes after the last thunder before resuming work
SUSPEND FIELD WORK IMMEDIATELY DURING:
• Tornado warnings
• Severe thunderstorm warnings
• Flooding conditions
• Extreme wind events
6. Wildlife and Environmental Hazards
Insects
Be alert for ticks, mosquitoes, bees, and wasps. Use insect repellent when appropriate and perform
thorough tick checks after all field work.
Cloudpoint Geospatial | Internal Use Only | Page 4

Cloudpoint Geospatial | Field Safety Guide cloudpointgeo.com | (877) 377-8124
Snakes and Other Wildlife
• Maintain a safe distance from all wildlife
• Never attempt to handle or approach animals
• Watch where hands and feet are placed — especially in tall grass, brush, and rocky areas
• Report all aggressive wildlife encounters to your supervisor
Poisonous Plants
Watch for and avoid contact with poison ivy, poison oak, and poison sumac. Wash any exposed skin
promptly with soap and water if contact occurs.
7. Water Hazards
When working near water bodies, drainage areas, or wet environments:
• Maintain safe distances from shorelines and embankments
• Be aware of slippery surfaces near water
• Do not enter water unless specifically authorized and trained
• Use personal flotation devices when required by project conditions
8. Working Alone (Lone Worker Safety)

Cloudpoint employees working alone must follow additional safety protocols to ensure their wellbeing
can be monitored effectively.
LONE WORKER REQUIREMENTS
• Notify your supervisor of your work location before starting
• Establish and follow a check-in schedule agreed upon with your supervisor
• Carry a fully charged communication device at all times
• Report any significant location changes to your supervisor promptly
• Do not enter unsafe areas alone
Work requiring special precautions or presenting elevated risk may require a second employee.
Supervisors will communicate these requirements in advance where possible.
Cloudpoint Geospatial | Internal Use Only | Page 5

Cloudpoint Geospatial | Field Safety Guide cloudpointgeo.com | (877) 377-8124
9. Utility and Infrastructure Hazards
Remain alert for overhead power lines, electrical equipment, underground utility markers, and active
construction activities at all field sites.
NEVER DO THE FOLLOWING UNLESS SPECIFICALLY TRAINED AND AUTHORIZED:
• Enter confined spaces
• Open utility structures or access covers
• Climb utility poles or structures
• Disturb or interfere with utility infrastructure
10. Vehicle Safety
Before Driving — Pre-Trip Inspection
Conduct a visual inspection before every field trip. Verify:
• Tires — no visible damage or low pressure
• Lights — headlights, brake lights, and turn signals functional
• Mirrors — properly adjusted
• Windshield — clean and unobstructed
• Fuel level — adequate for the assignment
While Driving
• Obey all traffic laws at all times

• Do not use handheld devices while driving
• Wear seatbelts at all times — all occupants
• Pull over safely before using phones, tablets, or GPS devices
11. Equipment Safety
Inspect all field equipment before use on every assignment. Equipment to inspect includes GPS units,
tablets, cameras, rangefinders, and measuring devices.
• Report damaged or malfunctioning equipment immediately to your supervisor
• Do not use equipment that appears unsafe or produces unexpected results
• Return equipment in the same condition it was issued
Cloudpoint Geospatial | Internal Use Only | Page 6

Cloudpoint Geospatial | Field Safety Guide cloudpointgeo.com | (877) 377-8124
12. Incident Reporting
All of the following must be reported to your supervisor immediately, regardless of severity:
REPORTABLE EVENTS
• Injuries — any injury to any person, however minor
• Vehicle accidents — including minor contact or near misses
• Near misses — events that could have caused injury or damage
• Property damage — to company, client, or third-party property
• Unsafe conditions — any hazard identified in the field
Prompt reporting allows hazards to be corrected and prevents additional incidents. There is no penalty
for reporting in good faith.
13. Emergency Procedures
EMERGENCY QUICK REFERENCE
Call 911 immediately for life-threatening emergencies
Then contact your supervisor and provide:
• Your exact location (address, coordinates, or landmark)
• Nature of the emergency

• Number of injured persons
• Any known hazards at the scene
Do not move injured individuals unless necessary to prevent further harm.
14. Stop Work Authority
All Cloudpoint employees have the authority — and the responsibility — to stop work whenever any of
the following conditions exist:
• Conditions have become unsafe
Cloudpoint Geospatial | Internal Use Only | Page 7

Cloudpoint Geospatial | Field Safety Guide cloudpointgeo.com | (877) 377-8124
• Required PPE is unavailable or inadequate
• Weather conditions create a hazard
• Traffic conditions present an excessive risk
• Any situation exists that could reasonably cause injury or property damage
No employee will be disciplined for exercising stop-work authority in good
faith.
When in doubt — stop, assess, and contact your supervisor.

Executive Summary
This document outlines the role definitions, responsibilities, key functions, and areas of focus
generally expected of staff designated as a Project Manager (PM) or Project Lead (PL) for the
successful delivery of Cloudpoint projects. These responsibilities and functions often overlap
and require regular communication between PM and PL. The PM has overall responsibility for
the delivery and success of the project, and therefore has ultimate decision-making
responsibility based on coordination with the Project Lead and relevant Team Lead.
Key Responsibilities and Focus Areas
1. Project Manager
A Project Manager (PM) is responsible for the overall planning, execution, monitoring, and
closure of a project. This role is generally broader and involves managing not just the technical
aspects of the project but also the business, budgeting, and communication aspects of the

project.
Key Responsibilities:
● Planning and Organizing: Develops the project plan, sets timelines, assigns resources,
and defines the project’s objectives.
● Scope Management: Ensures the project stays within the defined scope and manages
any changes in scope through formal processes.
● Budgeting: Manages the project budget, ensuring that costs stay within the approved
limit and making adjustments as necessary.
● Resource Allocation: Assigns the right people and resources to the project tasks and
ensures resources are effectively utilized.
● Risk Management: Identifies potential risks, develops mitigation strategies, and
proactively manages any issues that arise.
● Communication: Acts as the primary point of contact between stakeholders, sponsors,
and the project team. Provides regular status updates and ensures alignment on goals

and progress. The PM should be included on all communication with the Client, however
they do not have to be the initiator of all communication.
● Leadership and Decision-Making: Has the authority and responsibility to make
decisions, resolve conflicts, and adjust the course of the project if needed. Any issues
that arise during the course of the project should be brought to the attention of the PM
immediately.
● Quality Assurance: Ensures that there is a plan in place for reviewing quality standards
during the course of the project. Responsible for ensuring the project meets (preferably
exceeds) the expectations outlined in the contract. As this responsibility falls on the PM,
all deliverables must be reviewed by the PM prior to being sent to the Client. The PM

should be the default when sending deliverables, however they may delegate this as
they see fit.
● Closing: Ensures proper project closure, including documentation, final reporting, and
post-project analysis (lessons learned).
Focus Areas:
● Broad, strategic oversight.
● Budget and timeline management.
● Reporting to higher-level stakeholders (Team Lead and Client).
● Balancing multiple projects and managing interdependencies.
● Formal authority over project direction.
2. Project Lead
A Project Lead typically focuses more on the technical leadership of the project. They are often
responsible for managing a specific part or parts of the project or leading the team through the
technical aspects of execution. This role may be narrower in scope and more hands-on
compared to the Project Manager.
Key Responsibilities:

● Task and Team Management: Leads the day-to-day operations of the project team,
assigns tasks, monitors progress, and ensures technical deliverables are met.
● Technical Oversight: Provides expertise in the technical aspects of the project, often
making decisions on design, architecture, or development approach.
● Motivating the Team: Ensures the project team is motivated, has clear direction, and
has what they need to complete their tasks.
● Collaboration with PM: Works closely with the Project Manager to ensure alignment on
timelines, resources, and risks, but focuses on the team’s execution of tasks. All work
that goes to the Client must be reviewed by the PM first.
● Problem-Solving: Handles challenges or bottlenecks that arise during the day-to-day
work of the project team. Must inform PM of problems and risks immediately.

● Reporting: Provides regular updates on task completion, progress, and issues to the
Project Manager or stakeholders as appropriate.
● Mentorship: May mentor junior team members or provide guidance to ensure best
practices are followed.
Focus Areas:
● Project team management and execution of tasks.
● Technical decision-making.
● Ensuring daily operations align with project goals.
● Often more hands-on and involved in specific project work than PM.

● Focused on ensuring project deliverables meet requirements from a technical or team
perspective.
3. Key Differences
1. Responsibility:
○ Project Manager: Broad, responsible for the entire lifecycle of the project,
including scope, budget, risk, and communication with stakeholders.
○ Project Lead: Narrower, focused on leading the team and ensuring technical or
operational aspects are completed.
2. Decision-Making Authority:
○ Project Manager: Has authority over major project decisions, budget
adjustments, and scope changes.
○ Project Lead: Typically has authority over technical decisions but must defer to
the Project Manager for broader issues.
3. Stakeholder Management:
○ Project Manager: Manages communication with upper management, clients,
and sponsors.
○ Project Lead: Usually interacts more directly with the team and possibly middle
management or technical stakeholders.

4. Focus on Execution:
○ Project Manager: Focused on the big picture and the overall success of the
project.
○ Project Lead: More focused on the day-to-day tasks and team performance.
In summary, a Project Manager typically has a broader, strategic role involving oversight of the
entire project, while the Project Lead focuses on operational leadership and execution within
the project, often with a more hands-on approach.

sales and marketing team members. As a sales and marketing team member, you have a responsibility to

Section 3: Roles, Responsibilities & Deal Capacity
Outside Sales
These team members find leads and gather information. They are outbound hunters, the masters of
chasing down opportunities to feed into the pipeline. They focus on researching the leads to get contact
info and to see if they are qualified. They do initial sales calls and emails to prospects to learn about
needs and find out who the decision-maker is. They start the conversation, work with Team Leaders to
overcome objections, prepare quotes and proposals, follow-up regularly, and win deals.
Sales Capacity
Deal Capacity
Sales capacity is highly dependent on the size of deals and the client type, however we find it difficult for
sales leads to manage more than 25 active open deals at one time. If the number of deals exceeds this
limit it creates difficulties in effectively following up with prospects in a timely manner.

Deal Size Limits
Lead Generation
The new business development process involves three main sources for lead generation to fill the sales
pipeline.
● In-bound leads from the company web page or referrals
● Leads generated from marketing campaign activities (calls, emails, letters, etc.)
● Leads generated from events including conferences, showcases, webinars, or presentations

Purpose: To identify and nurture potential deals, even when they are highly uncertain or undeveloped.
1.1 Key Characteristics
● Represents very early sales activity—opportunities that are more potential than concrete.
● Sales team is educating stakeholders and planting the seed of a future solution.
● The aim is to educate prospects and ask them about their problems.
1.2 Lead Qualification Requirements
A Qualified Lead (QL) is a prospective customer who meets the necessary criteria outlined by the sales
and marketing staff. There is a difference between a Lead and a Qualified Lead. A lead is anyone that
expresses interest in our services, typically from an inbound channel such as a contact page or youtube
channel. However a QL is someone who passes through our filter of meeting the necessary criteria.

For example, if I’m trying to sell indoor mapping services to schools, I first have to identify leads that fit into
the Ideal Customer Profile (ICP). For more specific info see the ICP section of this playbook. Let’s say
that I’ve identified from my ICP that the perfect customers are schools with more than 5,000 students and
5 or more buildings on their campus. I might have received an inquiry from a principal reaching out to us
via the website and interested in our indoor mapping services, however, if he or she is in charge of a
school with only 300 students and has only 2 buildings on their campus, he would not be considered a QL.
However, I would still work with him or her to see if they meet other criteria and would be a good candidate
for other services we offer, however I would not have reached out to them directly (outbound methods)
since they did not meet my initial QL criteria.

A Qualified Lead (QL) must pass through our filter by meeting the following criteria:
● Industry/Demographic: Meets predefined industry, location, and size criteria.
● Identified Contact: Contains a specific person with a name and title.
● Authority: The contact has the authority to make or influence decisions.
The goal of the marketing and sales team is to move QLs along within the sales process to help them
become a customer success story. The QLs move through the sales process in stages, sometimes
skipping the first stage altogether. These stages (buckets) are defined as follows:
1.3 Lead Qualification Stages (IQL to SQL)
9

● Information Qualified Lead (IQL): Awareness stage. These leads meet our criteria but have not
yet engaged.
● Marketing Qualified Lead (MQL): Interest stage. The lead has expressed interest or responded
positively to initial contact.
● Sales Qualified Lead (SQL): Consideration stage. Leads that have identified a specific need and
have a potential for a sale within 12 months.
Information Qualified Lead (IQLs)- Awareness stage
These are leads that may potentially be interested in our services. The Lead Generation team finds their
contact information from a list or online. We really have no way to tell if they're interested but the fact is
that they meet our criteria for a qualified lead. IQLs are at the top of the sales funnel and there is the
greatest number of them out there compared to other leads. Sometimes these are considered cold leads.

These are typically discovered by means of Google searches or LinkedIn. Generally the lead generation
team finds the IQLs contact info and reaches out to them in the form of a mailer with follow up being
handled by the sales team. QLs are not considered IQLs until they have received some information from
us. Once that happens, they are ‘Aware’ of our products or services.
These leads are In the awareness stage, a prospect is researching a problem they might have. At this
stage, they are not necessarily looking for a solution to their problem. So the aim should be to educate
them and ask them about their problems.

You can convert IQLs to the next lead stage by inviting them to a webinar or sending them case studies,
offering them free consultations, etc. Many IQLs won’t engage, and you don’t need to worry them too
much as you can always send them marketing email newsletters.

Marketing Qualified Lead (MQLs)- Interest stage
A Marketing-Qualified Lead (MQL) is a potential customer who has been identified as meeting our target
criteria, has received information from us, and has expressed some type of interest or responded
positively to our initial contact. Sometimes MQLs may be referred to as prospects. The Marketing
designation simply means that they have expressed some type of interest or asked for some additional

information. They have expressed their interest by taking some kind of action to engage with us, such as
a past client who has done business with us, someone signing up for a free course, downloading a PDF, or
stopping by our booth at a trade show, or taking literature. The following channels are sources where our
MQLs come from:
● Positive response received
● Interest expressed
● Top to Middle of Funnel
● Some qualification criteria are met
● Past customers
● Content marketing
● SEO
● Paid Search
● Social
● Trade shows and events
● Customer referrals
Remember, not every lead that expresses interest is a Qualified Lead. They must meet the predefined
criteria. For example, a student from Canada looking for an Esri solution to assist with their doctoral thesis
is not a QL.
The interest stage means that they have a problem in mind and are looking for a solution to their problem.

It’s our job at this stage to convince them that our product or service could potentially solve their problem
and get them to the next stage of asking for a meeting to discuss.
However, those who have shown interest in how you might solve their problem might reach out to you by
giving more information about themselves like phone number, company information, and the exact
problem they are facing.

Sales Qualified Lead (SQL)- Consideration stage
Sales Qualified Leads (SQLs) are leads that are much closer to making a purchase than the others
described above. SQLs are people who have identified a specific need or problem and the potential exists
for a sale in the near future (within 12 months). A customer who we have done business with in the past
would still be considered an MQL but if they are inquiring about additional services at which point they
would become an SQL. You should prioritize SQLs at the top of your list when it comes to follow up
efforts. The last step in the lead qualification process is to move the SQL to a deal by identifying if they
meet all the following criteria to become a potential customer and convert into a deal.
● B- Budget, A- Authority, N- Need, T- Timeline
● Middle to Lower part of funnel

Purpose:

2.2 Discovery Meetings
The Discovery Meeting (sometimes referred to as a discovery call) typically includes the sales
representative and a team leader or technical specialist. There should ALWAYS be some knowledge of
who the customer is (something about them) and what they are looking for prior to this meeting. Be sure
to send a link to the appropriate Questionnaire prior to the discovery call if it applies.
This meeting is used to gain a better understanding of the customer’s needs and learn as much as
possible about how we can solve their problem and create wildly successful results. It should NEVER be

a one-sided demonstration of our team doing all the talking and never listening. It should be focused on
us asking questions as needed to learn the absolute most we can about the client. Have a presentation
prepared and come ready to talk about the company and your team, however if you don’t get the
opportunity to present it, that’s totally ok. Save it for later and you can always send that information in a
SOQ of proposal later on.
14

The four most important things to identify during the discovery call are as follows:
1. Cause- Find the cause of why the customer is reaching out to us.
a. “What caused you to reach out to us?”
b. “What are some of the pain points that you are experiencing?”
2. Outcome
a. “What would you envision the perfect outcome looking like once this project is completed?”
b. “How would you be leveraging the software or service?”
3. Obstacles
a. Are there any major obstacles you foresee that could keep this project from happening?”
4. Process- Who is involved with making the purchase decision and what is the time frame
a. “What does your decision process look like and how long might that take?”
b. “Who else do you see being involved with this process moving forward?”

Onsite meetings can prove to be extremely effective and valuable when done correctly and we want to

Section 5: Client Relations
Ongoing Client Relations
Once the deal has closed won, clients are transitioned to the Production Team via a Sales Handoff
Meeting. These meetings are fluid and scheduled as needed since the Team Leader is generally
knowledgeable of the deal already. During the project, the Operations Team will handle most customer
correspondence but it’s ok for sales reps to check in with customers as long as they are communicating
with project managers prior to reaching out.
After 6 months of post-project inactivity, without another open deal, the client will be placed back into the
IQL funnel for the Sales Team to pursue as a prospect.
New vs Existing Clients
Cloudpoint receives much of its work from past clients. When we use the term ‘Client’ here we are
referring to the Organization and not the individual. It is important to differentiate between new, current,

and past clients for the purpose of organizing our sales approach. The following definitions explain these
terms:
New Client
● An organization or department that has either never done business with Cloudpoint before or has
not had an active contract within the past 3 years.
Past Client
● An organization or department that has worked with Cloudpoint within the past 3 years but not
within the past 12 months.
Dormant Client
● Any organization or department that has worked with Cloudpoint in the past 5 years but has not
been contacted within the past 12 months.
Existing Client
● An organization or department that has an active contract with Cloudpoint or has had an active
contract within the past 12 months.

Section 9: Sales Tips, Tricks, & Best Practices
Best Practices
General Advice
● Trust- Selling professional services is largely about building trust-based relationships with potential
clients, and you can’t rush that.
● Persistence-The sale is often made after the fifth, seventh or even 12th attempt. If you give up after
two or three calls, you’re simply giving buyers away to the competition.
● Specialize- Don’t try to be all things to all people. Specialize and focus in the areas you add the
most value. Buyers love specialization because they equate it with expertise
○ Sales tip 1: Package your services like a product.
○ Sales tip 2: Position yourself as an expert.
○ Sales tip 3: Establish sales & service processes.
○ Sales tip 4: Provide great services that market themselves.
Stop-by’s
● Do not chew gum when making stops and introductions.

● Make sure to minimize distractions throughout the day so you are able to optimize your time and
make as many stops as possible.
● Sometimes you may have to look for the entrance and have to spend some time investigating
where to find the person. Don’t hesitate to knock on doors or open doors to do a little casual
investigating to find out where there is someone to talk to. Sometimes you may need to ring a call
button or something to get to speak with a person.
● When greeting people for the first time be sure to smile and have a pleasant attitude and
demeanor.
● Introduce yourself by name and the company and tell them why you are there, who you are looking
for, and ask if they are available. Sometimes that person is not at that location, in which case you
will need to get the address of the location to stop there later. Always thank the gatekeeper and be

sure to get his or her first name every time because you can use that in a follow-up email to your
contact.
● If the person is not available, ask for their contact information or business card and if it’s OK to
leave them with your materials to pass along to them. Always, always, always make sure you do
not leave without a business card or their contact info written down. Also, write down the first
name of the gatekeeper on the back of the business card to remember it later.
● Often the person that you are looking for may be housed at a separate facility or separate location
in which you should always ask for that location and go to that place to leave your information.
● If the person is available make sure you are brief and don’t take a lot of their time unless they are
genuinely interested. Always be ready to provide your brief pitch in case you run into the decision

maker unexpectedly. Regardless of the outcome of the conversation, be sure to ask them for any
referrals of others in their area who may be interested in your services.
35

● Following up is the most important part of the whole operation. We can make dozens of stops and
have quality conversations, however, if we are not following up, we are not going to make any
sales.
Email
● General guidelines for follow-up emails:
○ Briefly explain the problems that your solution or technology can solve for them.
○ Confirm that they are the correct contact at the organization to be talking to about this
matter.
○ Request time to meet to hear their needs, and introduce our company and services.
● Five email follow-up mistakes to avoid:
○ Not following up quickly. Many thought leaders believe that you should follow up on leads
five minutes after they send an inquiry through. But this is unrealistic, as you’re not sitting
by the phone all day, and you may be serving an international audience. However, it’s

important to follow up quickly. The longer you leave them, the less chance you’ll get a
response. Put systems in place to ensure you’re responding as quickly as possible.
○ Not focusing on the company. Many sales professionals make the mistake of putting all
their energy into the prospect. If you’re selling into large organizations, you need to be
engaging with multiple people. Always find out as much information about other
stakeholders and the buying process in order to accommodate all decision makers.
○ Not following up often enough. A study by Velocify found that 93% of converted leads are
reached by the sixth attempt. Make sure that you’re following up enough when the
relationship has begun. You’ll learn how to do this by adding value later in this guide.
○ Not using preferred channels. Anecdotally, 90% of the time prospects will want to hear from

sales reps by email. But some may prefer a phone call or other form of communication. If
they’d prefer a phone call over email, ask them what time is best to reach them.
○ Not tracking your metrics. Without measuring your sales performance, you won’t know if
what you’re doing is working. Use a CRM to measure the open and response rates of each
of your emails to see how each follow-up email performs.
LinkedIn
Examples of Personalized LinkedIn Messages
1. The Content Appreciation Connection (Post Engagement)
a. When to Use: Someone wrote a great article, post, or comment you found insightful.
b. Example: "Hi [Name], I really appreciated your recent post on AI ethics in
healthcare. Your point about 'data anonymization challenges' especially resonated
with me. I've seen similar issues in my work at [Your Company]. Would love to
connect and follow your future insights!".
36

2. The Event Follow-Up
a. When to Use: You met someone at a conference, webinar, or virtual event.
b. Example: "Hi [Name], It was great hearing your perspective on supply chain
optimization at the [Event Name] last week. Your tip about using predictive analytics
was spot on. I'm keen to connect with fellow professionals in this space. Hope to
stay in touch!".
3. The Shared Interest/Mutual Connection
a. When to Use: You have a common industry, alma mater, or connection.
b. Example: "Hi [Name], I noticed we both worked at [Mutual Company/University] and
share an interest in sustainable tech. I saw your recent work on [Project/Topic] and
was impressed. Would love to connect and exchange ideas.".
4. The "I'm Hiring" Approach (For Recruiters/Hiring Managers)
a. When to Use: You're looking for specific talent and see relevant skills.

b. Example: "Hi [Name], I'm impressed by your experience with React Native at [Their
Company]. We're expanding our mobile team at [Your Company] and looking for
someone with your skillset. Would you be open to a quick, no-pressure chat about
the role?".
5. The Value-Add Offer
a. When to Use: You have a relevant resource that solves a problem they face.
b. Example: "Hi [Name], I noticed you're hiring for GTM roles at your Series A startup.
We recently developed a Notion tracker for early-stage hiring that's helped similar
companies. Happy to share if it would be helpful for your team.".
6. Key Principles for Success
a. Be Specific: Mention concrete details from their profile, posts, or comments.
b. Offer Value First: Show how you can help or what you've learned from them.
c. Keep it Concise: Aim for 50-100 words; respect their time.

d. Clear Intent: Make your purpose (connection, insight, opportunity) clear.

chunks.content: 202- Showcase Events

The purpose of this SOP is to document our process for planning and executing showcase events. These events are usually partnered with Esri reps (but not required) to connect us with existing and potential clients face-to-face and build trusting, long-lasting relationships. Showcases began in 2015, with Cloudpoint staff presenting on various GIS topics to attendees invited via email. Attendees would come free of charge, and Cloudpoint would provide coffee, donuts, lunch, and presentation content.

This SOP applies to the Sales & Marketing team. It includes planning, advertising, setup, execution, and post-showcase follow-up procedures. The only thing not covered in this SOP is how to create the content/presentations, which will be left up to the presenters themselves.

The sales & marketing team will be responsible for carrying out the tasks outlined in this SOP and for reviewing and updating the details assigned to the Marketing Coordinator. Every showcase event will have a campaign manager (showcase manager) assigned. In most cases, this will be the business development manager, but it may also be a Director-level staff member.
Alignment is needed with Esri reps, usually their account managers, for the showcase target area. They can help with some contacts and finding the location Mailchimp access Squarespace access

chunks.content:
Copy this card to the desired location for tracking the Showcase execution progress
Create a New Campaign in Trello and Avaza following the SOP 201_SMA_001 Creating Campaigns
Select the potential dates and locations for the showcase.
It is highly preferred, to have Esri also present. Share and coordinate dates and locations with Esri.
Consult with SL and TL to work on agenda
Book venue, finalize start and end times
Confirm presenters from our staff and Esri
Schedule regular check-in meetings up to the time of the showcase. May not need them, but schedule anyway.
Create contact spreadsheet for invitation list
Setup the page to promote Showcase GIS Showcase Events for Local Government | Cloudpoint

chunks.content:
Contact list should be finalized (as much as possible)
Import Contact list to Pipedrive, update: label, activities, campaign
Create separate Audience in Mailchimp for the Showcase and import contacts
Setup the website for registrations
Add Agenda to webpage, must include: site address of showcase, a link to website for registering.
Create LinkedIn Event and share a post
Send postcard in the mail to contact list
Send 1st email invite 1 week after postcard to Audience in Mailchimp (as people register for the event, be sure to tag them as "Registered" in Mailchimp invite list so they won't receive any more invites)
Set up Email Drip to send every 1-2 weeks until Last Call email. This pattern will vary based on the scheduled date of the Showcase, holidays in the calendar, and sign-up rate.

chunks.section: Procedure- Start 45 days prior to event
chunks.content:
Sales staff calls everyone on the invite list leaving voicemails and following up with emails including a link to the webpage and possibly an attached pdf ad, but be wary of Spam Filters. One person should complete approximately 10 to 15 calls per hour including the follow up emails. Be sure to give them the web address of the registration page when leaving voicemails
Track all calls and emails in Pipedrive
Plan any ice-breaker activities, prize give aways, audience participation activities that will occur during the breaks or lunch times.

chunks.section: Procedure- Start 7 days prior to event
chunks.content:
Create attendee sign-in sheet for people to fill our their contact info onsite the day of the showcase (past templates available)
Create blank certificate sheets for people to take home from the showcase and sign for their CEU records. We do not offer formal PDH's but let attendees use the certificates as proof they attended.
Send Last Call email (Be sure to isolate the list to send only to those who are not tagged as "Registered")
Confirm catering orders, finalize catering details (who picks up lunch, how to pay for it, etc. Who is getting coffee and donuts and where, how to pay for)
Send Reminder email confirmation to those attending
Review packing list and make sure you have the necessary items
Make Google Photos Folder for pictures

chunks.section: On the Day of the event
chunks.content:
Remove registration link from website
Take plenty of photos for reference in later marketing materials (speakers, attendees, prize winners, staff setting up, interacting with clients, etc.)
Pass out certificates to participants any time after lunch. People that left early will not receive a certificate.
Pass out QR code for showcase feedback

Get all media (pics/videos) uploaded to the showcase google photos album
Create Showcase Show Notes blog summarizing the event (include pictures)
Double check official attendees list in Google Sheets and save in event folder
Add all attendees to Quarterly Newsletter
Update pictures and quotes on website page
Send thank you note or gift card ($25 or less) to Esri reps and any guest presenters / speakers
Make a final summary including notes of recommended changes for the next showcase

Click over to “Branding:" The next 10 steps follow:

chunks.content: 207- Campaign Execution

The purpose of this SOP is to outline the steps involved with the various methods Teams employs for Campaigns. These processes have proven effective over the years, though their success depends on numerous factors.
This SOP applies to all sales and marketing staff.
It is the responsibility of the Business Development Manager to update and maintain this SOP for future reviews, updates, and implementation.

Work with Marketing Coordinator to ensure the proper creation and planning steps are followed - https://trello.com/c/YG1deEp3/7-201-creating-campaigns

Generate your list of stop-bys
Contact the Esri Account manager for locations of planned stop-bys
Pre-stuff enough folders with the appropriate whitepages for the Campaign, and your business card.
Depending on the type of client and the distance between stops, 10 and 20 stops per day should be achievable. If this amount of stops is not achievable based on the driving distance between clients, a different marketing approach may be considered.
Sales work with Marketing to use ArcGIS Online to plan and optimize routes. ~insert link to dedicated Sales Routing Map/App here~
Sales staff work with Marketing staff to Create, and then later Mark Done, Stop-By Activities in PD
Ideally routes should be planned for one type of client, industry, or offering to stay focused on the message and not confuse marketing materials.

Plan to start earlier than normal on days of door-to-door marketing. Many of the industries and departments we serve start their day before 8AM.
Dress can be dependent to the client type (more formal for city halls, maybe a little less for trudging through PW buildings), however door-to-door stops should not be done in the stereotypical sales dress of khakis and a branded polo. Gentlemen should wear a sport coat, blazer, or appropriate suit jacket. Ladies should wear professional looking slacks or skirt, and a suit jacket or coat is also recommended. Overall appearance and hygiene should be well groomed and maintained to avoid distraction.
The vehicle used should be thoroughly washed the night before going out to make the stops. Also magnetic decals with the Cloudpoint logo should be put on the side of the vehicle prior to making the stops.

Make every effort to find the person you are looking for, often government campuses and buildings can be difficult to navigate (they should get Indoor maps!), introduce yourself positively and confidently. If they are not available get a card for confirming/updating contact info, and request the materials be passed along to them.
If the person is available, gauge their availability and interest, be as brief or in-depth as necessary. Plan follow-ups as needed. Regardless of the immediate outcome of the conversation, be sure to ask them for any referrals of others (departments, neighbors, etc.) who may be interested in our services.
Have a follow-up plan developed and properly scheduled after completing the planned stop-bys, and follow through with that plan. Follow Up!

Add/Update Pipedrive as soon as possible. The Marketing Team can assist with this. Tip: Slack them a photo of the business card while you are making stops.
Within 24 hours: send a follow email to each stop by, tailor the message to the result of the stop by.
Schedule a series of at least three follow-ups involving both emails and phone calls. This should all be outlined in the campaign plan details.

Create Activities in PD
Format letter content on CPG Letterhead
Format Mailing List for Mail Merge: this list could come from Pipedrive, from research for a Campaign, a Conference Attendee list, etc.
Execute Mail Merge
Print Letters
Stuff Envelopes, Label, Stamp, and Take to Post Office
Mark off checklist items in the Trello Campaign Card
Mark Activities Done in Pipedrive
Work with SL to schedule follow-up activities as needed
Update mailing addresses as needed if/when letters are returned

Generate the call list
Block out dedicated time on your calendar to make calls, generally this is more easily done at home or a more private location away from distractions
Prioritize and Categorize the order of the call list as needed
Create Activities in PD
Generate 30-60 second script for VoiceMail
Generate 10-20 second response to start conversation
Generate responses and rebuttals as needed
Generate notes regarding: anything specific to the Campaign, nearby past/current clients, similar projects, etc.
Prior to hitting dial quickly scan: name, job title, department, and additional Campaigns notes
Take thorough notes of call results
Logging calls and notes can sometimes be more quickly done in the GSheet of the call list itself, then update Pipedrive later.
Transpose notes to the "Note" field in the Activity for each person called in Pipedrive
Schedule follow-ups as needed

Update call sheet

chunks.content: 213- Conference Exhibiting Execution

The purpose of this SOP is to outline the general logistics of planning, exhibiting, and follow-up for a conference. NOTE: Every conference is different, with different timelines, requirements, and perks. Be aware that this SOP is very general.
This SOP applies to the Sales & Marketing team.

Pre-Conference Meeting: all CPG employees meet to review current clients, open deals, past clients, etc.
Review Agenda- note and prep for exclusive vendor times or events
Create Slideshow by copying that year's conference slidedeck template-save in that year's Conference folder-edit as needed
Share Slideshow with cloudpointgeospatial@gmail.com- this is a generic email that is solely used for the Conference Laptop

If no attendee list is provided from the conference, create a list from Pipedrive approximating known possible attendees. This is important for recognizing current/past clients, and attendees with open deals.
Conference Supplies are checked periodically throughout the year, but always good to double check swag and whitepages
Pre-conference Social Media
Send Pre-conference email- if a list is provided by the Organization
Day(s) prior: pull all needed materials to front of office for quick loading

Dress to Impress: Business Professional/Business Casual is always required. Cloudpoint gear is always acceptable, but not required.
Booth Position/Layout: "Open" set-up as much as possible: If on a corner remove the pipe and drape on the end of the row to open up the space. Moving the long table back or to the side, removing chairs, setting up the CPG podium in front with the monitor, lighted banners in the back of the booth are all best practices to increase the approachableness of your booth.
Swag: The Marketing Coordinator along with the "conference lead" should determine head of time an appropriate amount of swag to pack for each conference. Unless it is a 1 day event, DO NOT put all of the swag out at once. Pack away swag each night during multi-day events. Swag should be placed in orderly piles in the booth space. Upon return notify the MC if anything was depleted completely.

Demeanor: Be approachable! Stand up, smile, make good eye contact, be more interested in them than yourself. Don’t "hide" in the booth/behind the table. Try to have more than one person at the booth during peak exhibit hours.
Devices/Work: Do not 'work' at the booth. Clear your schedule to not conflict with exhibiting hours. Employees exhibiting at conferences are not expected to attend work related meetings. Talk with your manager if there is a major conflict. If a call must be taken, or email sent, try to conduct this business away from the booth. Limit cellphone usage to documenting leads/conference information at the booth. Do not "hide" or get distracted behind a screen.

Food/Drink: Biggest rule: BE CAREFUL, but do not starve yourself. We do not want to stain or damage any of our equipment or supplies. Do not sit and eat meals at the booth unless there is no other option given by the conference. Keep lids on drinks at all times. Be mindful of condensation.

Interacting: Exchange/Hand out as many business cards as possible. Document as much information as possible, as soon as possible regarding interactions with attendees: This could be on paper, notes in your phone, in a conference app, etc. Hand out as many whitepages as possible: pre-stuffing folders for 'niche' conferences may be helpful. Participate in as many "extra" activities as possible as long as there is adequate booth coverage: golf outings, awards banquets, social events, field trips, etc. Consider setting up a Client Dinner outside of the conference. If there are times when the exhibit space is not "open" to attendees, or everyone is in sessions, walk around the space and do not fear interacting with other vendors. Do not give away trade secrets. Survey for ideas: swag, displays, etc. Look for potential partnerships.

Put away, restock, and clean supplies as needed
Translate all notes to Pipedrive
Follow up individually with contacts: note that sometimes the conference goes longer than exhibiting and waiting until the next week to follow-up is acceptable
Post-conference Email: to all attendees if needed/list is provided, this also may be targeted to specific attendees based on job title or some other factor determined from the list
Review with S&M Team any other pertinent notes from the conference, especially anything that could help us next year: sponsorships, games, services/solutions to push, etc.

Standard Operating Procedure (SOP)
220-Marketing Content Review & Approval
Effective Date: 1/1/2026 Owner: VP of Sales Approved By: VP of Sales Applies To: All externally facing marketing and sales materials

This SOP defines a clear, consistent process for reviewing and approving marketing materials to ensure:
Brand consistency
Technical accuracy
Strategic alignment
Efficient decision-making without bottlenecks
The process is designed to scale as Cloudpoint grows while maintaining clarity around who owns the final approval .

This SOP applies to all external-facing content , including but not limited to:
Website pages and landing pages
Blog posts and thought leadership
Social media content
One-pagers and sales collateral
Case studies and white papers
Proposals (marketing components)
Email campaigns and newsletters
Event and conference materials

Owns brand standards, messaging, and visual consistency
Determines the approval tier for all content
Manages the review and approval workflow
Has final approval authority for Tier 1 content
Escalates all strategic alignment questions to the VP of Sales

Review and approve factual claims
Confirm the relevance of recipient lists when applicable

Owns strategic alignment and go-to-market consistency
Final approval authority for Tier 2 content
Resolves all escalated strategic questions

Includes marketing staff and leadership team
Provides strategic oversight for company-wide initiatives
Final approval authority for Tier 3 content
